An outlier-sensitivity lesson

Two points can tilt the fitted trend.

With spikes: +0.958 synthetic units / decade.

The selection changes the answer

Annual greening does not settle the summer question.

All months: +0.020 NDVI / decade; p < 0.001.
June–August: +0.003; p = 0.638.

The summer interval includes zero. This is inconclusive, not evidence of no change.

Evidence, scope and sources

The complete brief, with scope made explicit

The four required objectives

Challenge objectiveWhat the application does
Select Earth-science variables8 curated data series, a plain definition of each variable and question-led cards. Variables represent vegetation, surface temperature, air temperature, precipitation, soil moisture and global temperature anomaly.
Acquire data for a particular regionAdapters ingest MODIS through the Planetary Computer COG mirror, NASA POWER, GPCP and NASA GISTEMP. Regional NetCDF cubes are available for prepared regions; bounded requests can download new regional data. A visitor does not need an Earthdata account for these implemented adapters.
Generate and visualise a time seriesMonthly series, calendar-month anomalies, an optional 12-month running mean, fitted trend and 95% slope uncertainty. The user chooses a region, subarea, date range and months or season.
Estimate the rate and test significanceOLS slopes per decade, memory checks at monthly and yearly scales, confidence intervals, dependence-corrected Mann–Kendall tests, seasonal Sen slope, and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR on map cells. A non-significant interval is not described as proof of no change.

Background and optional considerations

Point in the challengeCoverage and interpretation
What, where, how much, and significanceVariable cards explain what is measured; the map locates the change; slopes and intervals quantify it; the verdict and cross-checks describe the evidence.
Regional changes can have opposite signsRegional maps and presets expose spatial differences. The recorded daytime LST cases show opposite signs in Central Europe and north-west India. Such differences do not establish causes and MODIS caveats still apply.
Land, ocean and atmospheric contextLand variables and near-surface atmospheric reanalysis are implemented. GISTEMP combines land stations with sea-surface observations globally. Dedicated ocean-depth products, pressure-level selection, evaporation and streamflow are outside the current implementation.
Example missions and modelsMODIS Terra/Aqua and MERRA-2 are used analytically. GPM IMERG is offered as contextual imagery, not the precipitation-trend input. OMI, AIRS and GLDAS are examples in the brief, not mandatory products and not implemented adapters here.
High-school, university and public audiencesPlain definitions, question-led selection, explanatory answers, “How we know”, a synthetic false-alarm lab and English, Spanish and Polish interfaces support these audiences. Classroom learning outcomes have not yet been evaluated.
Question-led discovery and demonstrations8 ready-made questions and prepared regions start an investigation. This deck includes a recorded real result plus three inspectable teaching examples on slide 4. The current app provides runnable noise and two-spike outlier examples.
Optional AI-assisted data discoveryThe current investigation is based on a curated catalogue, not news or literature search. Explanatory answers are fixed templates filled with computed values; optional AI-based discovery is not needed for the implemented workflow.
Temporal resolutions and long enough recordsThe prototype analyses monthly values. Its catalogue explicitly records product periods. Missing-data thresholds and period checks precede interpretation; monthly deseasonalisation accounts for the regular annual cycle.
Non-significant results can be usefulThe interface can return “No clear trend” and the answer explains an interval including zero. Longer records may help but are never presented as a guarantee of significance.
Nonlinear trends and seasonalityLinear trends meet the starting scope of the brief. The period matrix and season filters test sensitivity; the synthetic spike example shows that unusual points can influence the fitted slope. This is not a general nonlinear model or an automatic change-point detector.
Optional external hydrology toolsCUAHSI and the other supplied resources informed the brief; they are not integrated as analytical services. All resources supplied in the local research folder remain separate from implemented datasets.

How the pitch addresses the judging criteria

Relevance: all four objectives use NASA data. Validity: explicit uncertainty, tests and limitations. Creativity: combines exploration, sensitivity checks and statistical learning in one workflow. Impact: designed for independently checking local change, with user validation still ahead. Presentation: a real case, a clear test, a reproducible result.

Submission format follows the supplied guide: seven core slides, including the title slide, in English. The PDF includes only these seven English slides. Detail panels and Polish speaker notes support rehearsal. Format requirements come from the supplied official guide copies; this refresh verifies project facts against the recorded API, not a new rules audit.

Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
Join the Challenge
DetailsResourcesTeams
Event
2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge
Difficulty
Advanced
Subjects
Earth Science
Software
Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables. Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”


Background
Instruments on satellites observe many different aspects of the Earth system: on land, in the atmosphere, and in the oceans. Global models also use satellite instrument data and other kinds of data to examine and analyze the Earth system. One important reason for doing this is to observe and characterize changes in the Earth system. Changes, especially those moving in a particular direction over time – a trend – indicate both the processes causing such changes and the processes that will respond to them.

One complicating factor in this work is the wide variety of variables that can be studied. Another is that changes in a particular variable can move in one direction in one region and in the opposite direction in another, even when both trends are caused by the same process! So there are two important parts to this problem: finding variables that are trending, from simple ones like temperature and rainfall to more complex ones like evaporation or streamflow; and analyzing trends in particular regions of the land, ocean, or even levels of the atmosphere.

Instruments such as the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), the Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI), the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS), and the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) provide analyzable variables. Global models – notably the Modern Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2) and the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) – provide many more. Finding, analyzing, and relating significant trends to the processes causing them is one of the most important uses of NASA Earth science data.

Objectives
A successful response to this challenge will bring together several important elements.

The first is to identify Earth science variables of interest that can be investigated for potential trends. As the Background notes, NASA and other space agencies offer numerous variables, some familiar and some more specialized for use by particular branches of science.

The second is to acquire the data variables for a particular region, since most trends in the data will not be global – though some trends can be!

The third is to generate and visualize a time series for the variable and region of interest over a long enough period of time to allow statistical analysis.

The final element of the challenge is to perform a basic statistical analysis of that time series, indicating the rate of change over time, and to test the trend’s significance using methods such as a t-test, the Mann-Kendall test, or confidence intervals.

Data sites offer tools that generate time series, and statistical analysis packages provide basic significance testing. A response that does both the visualization and the analysis meets the full scope of this challenge.

Potential Considerations
You may (but are not required to) consider the following:

Audience

This challenge involves science data and statistical analysis, so the likely audience is high school and college students, along with members of the public who have some scientific background.
Providing simple definitions of the variables would help these users considerably.
The concept is to help the users become data detectives – finding variables of interest, then determining whether those variables show a trend and whether that trend is significant.
Approach

Users could potentially respond to a short series of questions about what or where they would like to investigate, and then the answers to the questions would allow searching of related data variables. It would be highly useful to provide a couple of demonstration examples that the user could watch and would help them understand how the tool works.
While not required, SI could be useful here to identify data with the potential to show trends in particular areas, drawing on either news articles and research papers or the characteristics of a region such as a desert, rain forest, tidal estuary, or the atmosphere above a large city.
Working with the data

Earth science data are available at several different temporal resolutions – hourly, 3-hourly, daily, and monthly. For this challenge, daily and monthly data are likely the easiest to process.
Finding a trend is interesting even if it doesn’t reach the level of significance. Sometimes all a trend needs to become significant is a longer period for the data to be acquired.
Consider looking for publicly available tools for plotting hydrological data offered by outside organizations like the Consortium of Universities for the Advancement of Hydrologic Science, Inc. (CUAHSI).
Trend analysis with Earth science data can be complex. Trends can be non-linear, and some are not evident unless regular cycles, such as the seasonal cycle, are removed. More complex trend analyses are beyond the scope envisioned for this challenge; detecting and analyzing linear trends would be a great start.

For data and resources related to this challenge, refer to the Resources tab at the top of the page. More resources may be added before the hackathon begins.

Implemented application inventory

Globe explorer

  • MapLibre 3D globe, NASA GIBS Blue Marble and historical imagery, Natural Earth borders, and a Yale Bright Star Catalogue background.
  • Imagery choices: true colour, monthly vegetation, monthly land-surface heat, monthly air temperature and daily IMERG rainfall. These are contextual layers; they are not interchangeable with the analytical data sources.
  • Trend maps, annual anomaly frames, play/pause through years, coordinated imagery date and month selection, data opacity and data visibility controls.
  • FDR-based fading, cell-level hover statistics, cell clicks, world/region navigation and separate global-monthly visual layers for datasets without a global statistical cube. Global GISTEMP can also find and save non-overlapping areas with similar average mapped trend rates; this compares rates, not whole climates.
  • Rectangle selection, dataset-specific extent limits, reuse of existing cubes, asynchronous regional downloads with progress, result cards and a mini time-series chart.
  • “Full analysis” carries the selected area into Detective.
  • New areas are recorded on the server; each visitor controls which saved places are visible. Other visitors’ areas can be shown, and hiding a place does not delete it for everyone.
  • Tile/frame prefetch, in-place image changes, fading between imagery dates and softened polar imagery support a smooth visual experience.

Detective

  • 8 question cards with definitions; a catalogue of prepared and available custom regions; dataset availability checks.
  • Start/end-year dropdowns and timeline controls, all-year and seasonal selections, clicked grid cells and rectangle subareas.
  • A trend map with a physical-unit scale, missing-data indication, FDR fading and a separate valid-month coverage view.
  • Plain-language answers grounded in the computed result: trend direction and rate, overall change, ordinary year-to-year variability, spatial distribution, sensitivity and a source-specific caveat.
  • Verdicts distinguish detected trends, an interval including zero, period-dependent direction, period-dependent significance and insufficient data.
  • OLS interval and p-value from monthly and yearly memory checks, corrected Mann–Kendall, Sen slope, sample sizes, valid data share and overlapping-window sensitivity.
  • Monthly anomaly and running-mean charts, fitted trend and confidence fan; a typical seasonal-cycle chart.
  • An interactive start/end-year matrix. Clicking a cell updates the selected period.
  • Cross-source comparisons on common areas and periods: POWER/GISTEMP temperature, POWER/GPCP rainfall and Terra/Aqua surface temperature; identification of the largest mapped warming rate in the relevant answer.
  • Source product, citation, provider, resolution, licence and caveats visible alongside the analysis.
  • CSV time-series export, JSON evidence export and a reproducible URL hash for the variable, region, period, months and subarea.

False-alarm laboratory

  • Clearly labelled synthetic AR(1) monthly data with no underlying continuous trend; controls for years and memory; new seeded examples.
  • Naive and corrected significance tests with the same observed synthetic series, so users can see the role of persistence.
  • A 200-run experiment with counts, proportions, 95% Wilson intervals, and three bars: naive result, corrected result and the fixed nominal 5% reference.
  • Two deliberately injected late spikes, generation of new examples and comparison with the original series. The lesson demonstrates OLS sensitivity to known synthetic outliers, without recommending automatic removal of real extremes.
  • Source-specific caution around Amazon precipitation is shown in the real analysis, separately from the simulations.

Resilience and rollout status

The current local build assembles air temperature, land surface temperature, precipitation and root-zone soil wetness for a common area and period. It supports CSV/JSON export, a printable brief and opening the same selection in Detective. Its use cases cover civilian and defence infrastructure. This is historical regional exposure, not a facility risk score or operational forecast.

Public demo checked 2026-11-15 11:12 CET. The public Resilience UI loaded all four cards through its compatibility fallback; the dedicated endpoint returned 404. The deck records the current local API and UI, with source hashes; it does not restart or deploy the public server.

Development roadmap

A guided tour is being developed separately; an integrated tour, fire-history analysis, daily heat metrics and a space-weather panel are not claimed as completed presentation features.

Access, experience and engineering

  • English, Spanish and Polish dictionaries. The language selector is hidden beneath the supplied icon at the lower left, and switching re-renders existing results without page reload or recomputation.
  • Preserved language preference, URL-based language fallback, mobile layouts, light and dark themes, keyboard controls, reduced-motion support and one tooltip style. A formal screen-reader audit has not been completed.
  • Python/FastAPI API; NumPy, SciPy and xarray calculations; NetCDF regional caches; source adapters; statistical and API tests; localisation regression checks.
  • The browser frontend uses JavaScript, MapLibre, Leaflet and Plotly without a build step.
  • Public demo mode applies job and simulation limits. Optional pruning bounds retained custom data; it is disabled by default locally.
  • Answers are deterministic templates, not generated scientific findings. Every displayed number is calculated from a cited dataset or explicitly synthetic experiment.
Not claimed: GPU acceleration, full global coverage for every variable, automatic causal attribution, operational forecasting, a pressure-level explorer, automatic change-point discovery, measured classroom impact or a completed external scientific validation.

Products, credits and scientific limits

Important limitations. MODIS values are read at native resolution and screened with pixel reliability / QC_Day before aggregation to 0.1°. NDVI screening retains good and marginal pixels. Composite-to-month boundaries remain approximate, and satellite orbit drift after 2022 can affect interpretation. POWER uses MERRA-2 reanalysis; its variables share a model source. GPCP adds a coarse 2.5° satellite–gauge rainfall comparison, with some shared observational inputs. GISTEMP uses spatial smoothing. The selected-period anomaly baseline is not a universal fixed reference period. Statistical significance alone neither validates a source artefact nor identifies a cause.

All analytical datasets

Vegetation greenness (NDVI)

NDVI compares red and near-infrared light reflected by plants; higher values mean denser, healthier green vegetation (−0.2 water/bare … 0.9 dense forest).

Product: MOD13A1 v061 (Terra, 16-day, 500 m)
Provider: NASA LP DAAC; COG mirror on Microsoft Planetary Computer
Period: 2001–2024
Units: NDVI (unitless); trend: NDVI per decade

Didan, K. (2021). MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 Global 500m SIN Grid V061. NASA EOSDIS LP DAAC. doi:10.5067/MODIS/MOD13A1.061

Licence: NASA EOSDIS data: no restrictions on reuse (NASA Earth Science Data Policy)

  • Monthly value = mean of 16-day composites starting in that month, read at the native 500 m resolution and averaged to 0.1°.
  • Quality-screened: pixels the MODIS quality layer marks as cloudy, snow/ice or missing are removed first; a cell needs at least 20% good pixels in a composite.
  • Terra's orbit drifted after 2022; the default period stops at 2024.
  • A change in NDVI can come from land-use change (clearing, irrigation), not only from climate.

Daytime land surface temperature

How hot the ground/canopy surface is around 10:30 local time, measured from space in clear-sky conditions – not the air temperature you feel.

Product: MOD11A2 v061 (Terra, 8-day, 1 km)
Provider: NASA LP DAAC; COG mirror on Microsoft Planetary Computer
Period: 2001–2024
Units: °C; trend: °C per decade

Wan, Z., Hook, S., Hulley, G. (2021). MODIS/Terra Land Surface Temperature/Emissivity 8-Day L3 Global 1km SIN Grid V061. NASA EOSDIS LP DAAC. doi:10.5067/MODIS/MOD11A2.061

Licence: NASA EOSDIS data: no restrictions on reuse (NASA Earth Science Data Policy)

  • Only clear-sky observations exist: cloudy months contribute fewer values (see coverage).
  • Monthly value = mean of 8-day composites at the native 1 km resolution; pixels the quality layer marks as not produced or with LST error above 2 K are removed first.
  • Terra's overpass time drifted after 2022; the default period stops at 2024.

Afternoon land surface temperature (Aqua)

Same measurement as the Terra daytime surface temperature, but from the Aqua satellite passing around 13:30 local time; its orbit was kept stable until 2022, so it is a useful cross-check.

Product: MYD11A2 v061 (Aqua, 8-day, 1 km)
Provider: NASA LP DAAC; COG mirror on Microsoft Planetary Computer
Period: 2003–2024
Units: °C; trend: °C per decade

Wan, Z., Hook, S., Hulley, G. (2021). MODIS/Aqua Land Surface Temperature/Emissivity 8-Day L3 Global 1km SIN Grid V061. NASA EOSDIS LP DAAC. doi:10.5067/MODIS/MYD11A2.061

Licence: NASA EOSDIS data: no restrictions on reuse (NASA Earth Science Data Policy)

  • Aqua starts in mid-2002; the cube starts in 2003 (first complete year).
  • Afternoon surface temperature differs from morning (Terra) values; compare trends, not levels.
  • Aqua's orbit also began drifting after 2022.
  • Quality-screened like the Terra product: pixels not produced or with LST error above 2 K are removed.

Air temperature at 2 m

Monthly mean air temperature two metres above the ground, from the NASA MERRA-2 reanalysis (a model that assimilates observations).

Product: NASA POWER monthly T2M (MERRA-2)
Provider: NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project
Period: 1981–2025
Units: °C; trend: °C per decade

NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER Project, funded through the NASA Earth Science/Applied Science Program; MERRA-2 (Gelaro et al., 2017, J. Climate).

Licence: NASA POWER data: free to use, acknowledgement requested

  • Reanalysis = model constrained by observations; not a direct satellite measurement.

Precipitation

Average amount of rain and snow reaching the ground per day, from MERRA-2 corrected with observed precipitation.

Product: NASA POWER monthly PRECTOTCORR (MERRA-2, bias-corrected)
Provider: NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project
Period: 1981–2025
Units: mm/day; trend: mm/day per decade

NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER Project; MERRA-2 bias-corrected precipitation (Reichle et al., 2017).

Licence: NASA POWER data: free to use, acknowledgement requested

  • Precipitation varies a lot year to year: long periods are needed before a trend is detectable.
  • Independent check: GPCP v2.3 (satellites and rain gauges) for the same area and period is shown with every result.

Precipitation (GPCP, satellites and gauges)

Monthly rain and snow from the Global Precipitation Climatology Project, which merges microwave and infrared satellite estimates with rain-gauge analyses (GPCC). It does not come from the MERRA-2 model.

Product: GPCP v2.3 monthly (satellite–gauge analysis)
Provider: NASA GSFC and University of Maryland (GPCP); distributed by NOAA PSL / NCEI
Period: 1988–2025
Units: mm/day; trend: mm/day per decade

Adler, R.F. et al. (2018). The Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) Monthly Analysis (New Version 2.3) and a Review of 2017 Global Precipitation. Atmosphere 9, 138. doi:10.3390/atmos9040138. Data: doi:10.7289/V56971M6

Licence: NOAA NCEI Climate Data Record: no usage restrictions

  • Coarse 2.5° grid: a small area uses only a few cells, or the nearest one.
  • Starts in 1988: earlier years rely on an infrared-only index and are less homogeneous.
  • Partly independent of MERRA-2: different satellites and gauge analysis, but over Africa MERRA-2 land rain is rescaled to the GPCP climatology (Reichle et al. 2017).

Root-zone soil wetness

How full the soil water store is in the root zone (top ~1 m): 0 = completely dry, 1 = saturated. Modelled by MERRA-2.

Product: NASA POWER monthly GWETROOT (MERRA-2)
Provider: NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project
Period: 1981–2025
Units: fraction (0–1); trend: fraction per decade

NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER Project; MERRA-2 land surface (Reichle et al., 2017).

Licence: NASA POWER data: free to use, acknowledgement requested

  • Model estimate: irrigation and groundwater pumping are not represented.
  • Planned independent check: SMAP (2015–) or GRACE water storage (needs Earthdata Login).

Surface temperature anomaly (GISTEMP v4)

Difference between the monthly surface temperature and its 1951–1980 average, combining weather stations on land and ships/buoys at sea.

Product: GISTEMP v4, 1200 km smoothing, GHCNv4 + ERSSTv5
Provider: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies
Period: 1951–2025
Units: °C (anomaly vs 1951–1980); trend: °C per decade

GISTEMP Team (2026). GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP), version 4. NASA GISS. Lenssen et al. (2019, 2024).

Licence: NASA GISS data: free to use with citation

  • Grid cells far from stations are filled from neighbours up to 1200 km away; polar and early-period values are less certain.
  • Small regions contain only a few 2° cells.

Statistical methods

  • Deseasonalisation: Each calendar month's mean over the selected period is subtracted (anomalies).
  • Trend: Ordinary least squares slope of the anomalies, reported per decade.
  • Uncertainty: Two memory corrections: month to month (AR(1) for the actual sampling, bias-corrected; Santer et al. 2000) and year to year (the same test on yearly means). The p-value is the larger of the two and the 95% interval covers both, so a trend counts only if both agree.
  • Cross check: Seasonal Mann–Kendall with the Hirsch & Slack (1984) correction for dependent months, and Mann–Kendall on yearly means with the Hamed & Rao (1998) correction; the larger p is shown. Seasonal Sen slope.
  • Calibration: Checked on synthetic series without a trend: with month-to-month memory up to 0.9, seasons and gaps, at most about 6% are called significant (the target is 5%). Slow decade-long swings remain hard: 5–12% instead of 12–39% before this correction.
  • Map multiple testing: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate across map cells, q = 0.05 (Wilks 2016).
  • Period choice: The map correction covers grid cells, not the choice of period, season or variable: the more combinations you try, the more likely one looks significant by chance. The squares in “Does it hold?” overlap, so they are not independent repeats.
  • Regional mean: cos(latitude)-weighted mean of cell anomalies; months with < 50% area coverage are dropped.
  • Minimum data: A trend is computed only if at least 70% of the selected months are valid.

The chart fan pivots at mean time using the slope bounds; it is not a prediction interval. Cross-source agreement does not establish causation or complete independence of the observations.

Santer et al. (2000); Hirsch & Slack (1984); Hamed & Rao (1998); Sen (1968); Benjamini & Hochberg (1995); Wilks (2016). The exact method notes are included in the evidence download.

  • No official NASA endorsement is implied.

The HTML works offline. Its figures are recorded results, not a live connection to NASA. The external application link opens the current demo. Source file hashes, request parameters, numerical payloads, methods and citations are embedded in this HTML and saved in evidence.json.

A short, reproducible live demonstration

  1. Open the live app in English. On Globe, inspect the GISTEMP global trend and its physical-unit legend.
  2. Open Detective, select “Warmer air?”, Central Europe, 1981–2025, all months. Inspect the slope, 95% interval and “How we know”.
  3. Inspect the start/end matrix: 133 of 136 windows have the same direction; 45 have that direction and p < 0.05.
  4. Open False alarms. Set 10 years and memory 0.7; run 200 series. The recorded seed-1000 experiment produced 83 naive alarms and 5 corrected alarms. These are simulation outcomes, not Earth observations.
  5. In “Can two spikes tilt a trend?”, compare without spikes. The current recorded example moves from +0.958 to -0.067 synthetic units per decade when the known injected spikes are removed.
  6. Return to Globe, draw a small area already inside Central Europe, choose air temperature and analyse. Open the full investigation, then export CSV/JSON.
  7. Open the lower-left language icon and switch to Polish or Spanish. Existing selections and calculated results are preserved.

Additional recorded teaching example

Central Europe NDVI, 2001–2024: all months +0.020 [0.012; 0.029] per decade, p < 0.001; June–August +0.003 [-0.009; 0.014], p = 0.638. Both use the same region and source. The native pixels are quality-screened before aggregation. The contrasting seasonal results do not attribute greening to climate.

What is still to validate

  • Extend quality sensitivity checks to other MODIS masks, spatial aggregation and satellite orbit drift.
  • Investigate precipitation disagreements and shared-input limitations beyond the current GPCP comparison.
  • Test slow climate variability beyond the synthetic memory scenarios already covered.
  • Run usability sessions with learners and educators, including keyboard and screen-reader evaluation.
  • Extend data products and spatial support only with corresponding scientific and engineering validation.
